title: The water footprint of water conservation using shade balls in California
authors: Haghighi E, Madani K, Hoekstra AY
scale: Los Angeles reservoir (Sylmar, CA), surface area ~710,000 m2, >96 million 100 mm HDPE shade balls released August 2015
dose: Full surface cover with plastic shade balls
result: Saving an estimated 1.15 million m3/yr of evaporation with 96 million HDPE balls costs 0.25-2.9 million m3 of water to make them (ball thickness 1-5 mm, water footprint 0.05-0.19 m3/kg HDPE), so the balls must stay 0.2-2.5 years for net water savings. The paper reports no algae or water-quality data and calls shade-ball control of water quality an open question.
env_effects: Large manufacturing water footprint; plastic production and waste.
key_details: Short perspective-style analysis using water-footprint accounting (consumptive use only) for HDPE production. The total HDPE mass needed to cover a given area depends only on ball thickness, not diameter. The balls were deployed partly to prevent algal-bloom water-quality deterioration, but whether they worked for that is stated as unresolved; some experts hypothesised a thermal-blanket effect promoting bacterial growth. Thin, lightweight balls may drift and expose warmed water, increasing evaporation. The water saving figure is the Los Angeles officials' estimate, not a measurement.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record's figures are rounded: 96 million balls (not ~100 million), 1.15 million m3/yr saved (not ~1.2), footprint 0.25-2.9 million m3, and payback 0.2-2.5 years depending on thickness.

title: Controversy over the Use of "Shade Covers" to Avoid Water Evaporation in Water Reservoirs
scale: Review of suspended shade cloth covers and floating shade objects on agricultural reservoirs
result: Review: studies of suspended shade-cloth covers report evaporation cuts close to 85% and a 'dramatic limitation of algal blooms', but the evidence base is scarce; the author's own unpublished pool test (one uncovered vs two shade-ball pools, June-September 2014) found clearer water and up to 90% less evaporation under shade balls.
env_effects: Polyethylene shade objects: high energy and raw-material cost, recalcitrant residues, possible endocrine-disrupting leachates after long sun exposure (~10 years), unstudied microplastic release, visual pollution.
key_details: Short single-author narrative review (Sustainability, 2021) of suspended shade-cloth covers and floating shade objects (balls, hexagons) on reservoirs. No quantitative algal data beyond citing Martinez-Alvarez et al. for 'dramatic limitation of algal blooms'. Includes an unpublished, unreplicated pool experiment (1 control, 2 covered pools) measured by turbidity and OD600 rather than algal counts. Main point is the unresolved cost and plastic-waste trade-off.
fulltext_discrepancy: None material; record should note the algae evidence is second-hand plus one small unpublished pool test.

title: Experimental assessment of shade-cloth covers on agricultural reservoirs for irrigation in south-eastern Spain
authors: Martínez Álvarez V, Maestre-Valero JF, Martín-Górriz B, Gallego-Elvira B
scale: One agricultural irrigation reservoir, Segura basin, SE Spain: 2,400 m2 surface, 5 m deep, 11,920 m3; uncovered year 1 (2007-08) vs covered year 2 (2008-09); no simultaneous control reservoir
dose: Black polyethylene suspended shade-cloth cover (<1% solar transmission); cost EUR 7.80/m2 (EUR 5.30 structure + 2.50 cloth)
result: Evaporation fell close to 85% (84% used in economics). Under the cover photosynthesis dropped massively and algal growth was highly limited (chlorophyll shown only in a figure, 0-30 ug/L axis); farmers reported a 90% cut in filter cleaning.
env_effects: Near-total light removal suppresses all photosynthesis; cost/benefit analysed.
key_details: Before/after design on a single reservoir: year 1 uncovered (used to validate an open-water evaporation model), year 2 covered; monthly samples at 1-4 m for algal cells (inverted microscope) plus YSI profiles of EC, chlorophyll and turbidity. No numerical chlorophyll values are given in text; the 90% filtration benefit is an anecdotal landholder report. Discounted cash-flow analysis found the cover not economically viable when saved water is valued at purchase price (EUR 0.15-0.50/m3), but viable where water shortage limits cropped area.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record right in substance; adds the unreplicated before/after design, the cost, and that algae reductions are shown only graphically.

title: The Pond Dye, Aquashade, Does Not Prevent Cyanobacterial Off-Flavors in Pond-Grown Channel Catfish
organism: Planktothrix perornata and pond phytoplankton; channel catfish
scale: 6 earthen ponds (~0.05 ha, ~0.7 m deep, ~325 m3), 3 treated vs 3 untreated, randomly assigned; Stoneville, Mississippi, 1988
dose: Aquashade 1.0 uL/L on June 8, then monthly through September 8 (four treatments)
result: Chlorophyll-a did not differ between dyed and undyed ponds (early season 152 vs 145 ug/L; late season 117 vs 208 ug/L, P = 0.140). Odorous cyanobacteria appeared in 15 of 42 samples across all six ponds, and at the end two ponds per treatment had off-flavored fish.
env_effects: No difference in nitrite, ammonia or aeration hours. About half the dye was gone 10 days after each application, possibly through anaerobic degradation in sediment.
key_details: Randomized pond trial with 3 treated and 3 control commercial-style catfish ponds, sampled biweekly for chlorophyll-a, nitrogen and dye concentration, with microscopic checks for odour-producing algae and flavor tests. Late-season chlorophyll-a looked lower in dyed ponds (117 vs 208 ug/L) but did not differ statistically because of large pond-to-pond variation. Nine of the 15 samples with odorous cyanobacteria came from dyed ponds and six from undyed ponds; three ponds had very strong off-flavors (two dyed, one control). The dye's major absorbance is 550-680 nm, peaking at 630 nm.
fulltext_discrepancy: The record says Planktothrix was present in two ponds of each treatment; the full text says odorous cyanobacteria (Planktothrix perornata or Microcystis) were found in all six ponds, and two ponds per treatment had unacceptable off-flavor fish at the end. The late-season chlorophyll-a was 44% lower in dyed ponds but not significantly so, so effect_pct 0 means no significant effect rather than an identical value.

title: The Effect of the Dye Aquashade® on Water Quality, Phytoplankton, Zooplankton, and Sunshine Bass, Morone chrysops×M. saxatilis, Fingerling Production in Fertilized Culture Ponds
authors: Ludwig GM, Perschbacher PW, Edziyie R
venue: Journal of the World Aquaculture Society
scale: 9 fertilized 0.04-ha ponds (~70 cm deep), Stuttgart, Arkansas, 2006; 3 early-dye, 3 late-dye, 3 control, randomly assigned
dose: Aquashade 4.8 mg/L (label rate for macrophyte control is 2 mg/L), applied at filling (May 18) or at day 25 (June 12)
duration: 47 days from stocking to fingerling harvest
result: Mean chlorophyll-a over the whole study was significantly higher in dyed ponds (86.5 early, 75.5 late) than in controls (66.7 ug/L; P = 0.02); cyanobacteria densities did not differ among treatments. Respiration, gross and net primary productivity, fish size and condition did not differ.
env_effects: Two control ponds had the lowest fish survival (4.4% and 1.8%) and the highest unionized ammonia (0.14 and 0.10 mg/L average, up to 0.48 mg/L) and pH up to 9.73; differences in pH and unionized ammonia among treatments were not statistically significant.
key_details: Randomized pond trial with three treatments (dye at filling, dye at day 25, no dye), n = 3 ponds each, fertilized with rice bran and stocked with sunshine bass larvae at 15,000 per 0.04 ha. Water chemistry was sampled throughout, with phytoplankton identified to species. Secchi visibility did not differ overall (44.2, 52.3, 47.4 cm). Chlorophyll-a was higher, not lower, in dyed ponds; macrophytes (Najas sp.) were still present at draining. effect_pct -29.7 is computed from 86.5 vs 66.7 ug/L (early dye vs control).
fulltext_discrepancy: Dose was 4.8 mg/L, not 4 mg/L. The record says there were few differences in chlorophyll-a; in fact chlorophyll-a was significantly higher in dyed ponds than in controls (P = 0.02). The record's claim that undyed ponds reached harmful pH/ammonia is from two control ponds only and was not statistically significant.

title: Aquashade(R) Treatment of Channel Catfish Ponds
venue: North American Journal of Fisheries Management
organism: Pond phytoplankton, underwater weeds, channel catfish
result: Dye turned water blue but did not appreciably change Secchi depth; chlorophyll-a and weed cover did not differ from controls. Dye concentration fell ~0.75 mg/L per month through seepage.
env_effects: Dusk dissolved oxygen lower in treated ponds; no water-quality improvement.

title: Evaluation of Transparency and Light Attenuation by Aquashade™
authors: Madsen JD, Getsinger KD, Stewart RM, Skogerboe JG, Honnell DR, Owens CS
scale: 3-m deep outdoor tanks with reservoir water
result: In filtered lake water, 1 and 5 mg/L cut transparency by ~10% and ~30%; with clay turbidity, 1 mg/L had no significant effect and 5 mg/L cut it 31%. Dye absorbs 550-650 nm (peak ~630 nm); at the allowed 1 mg/L the light effect is small.
env_effects: Visibility stays above swimming standards at label rates.

title: Illuminating the Impact of a Floating Photovoltaic System on a Shallow Drinking Water Reservoir: The Emergence of Benthic Cyanobacteria
authors: Sandrini G, Wagenvoort AJ, van Asperen R, Hofs B, Mathijssen D, van der Wal A
scale: Kralingen drinking-water storage reservoir, Rotterdam (shallow); sun-tracking FPV of 0.95 ha (24% of surface, 1.00 MWp) installed April 2020; under-array site compared with open water ~35 m away, diving surveys before (2019) and after
result: Direct light under the array peaked at 23% of open water in summer; benthic cyanobacterial mats (Gomphosphaeria, then Phormidium) developed under the FPV while Chara and other macrophytes disappeared there. Planktonic phytoplankton composition was generally very similar under the array and in open water.
env_effects: Benthic mats produced geosmin up to 20 ng/L (odour threshold ~5 ng/L), 2-MIB, anatoxin-a (0.014 ug/g) and microcystins (8.8 ug/g wet weight in 2022), though not problematic for the treatment plant; loss of Chara; heavy Dreissena biofouling on floats; DO and temperature little affected.
key_details: Field monitoring of one reservoir with a single FPV array (no replicate reservoirs); comparisons are before/after plus under-array vs open-water points. Light modelling explained the shift: bottom light under the array fell below the ~3% surface level assumed for Chara but stayed above the 1% level for cyanobacteria. No benthic cyanobacterial mats were found in July 2019 before installation. Overall phytoplankton biovolume decreased but cyanobacteria became relatively more abundant over time. Evides (the utility) authors.
fulltext_discrepancy: None material; record lacked the toxin and odour numbers and the fact that planktonic phytoplankton hardly changed.

title: Effects of floating photovoltaic systems on water quality of aquaculture ponds
authors: Wang T-W, Chang P-H, Huang Y-S, Lin T-S, Yang S-D, Yeh S-L
freshwater_or_marine: both (freshwater prawn and tilapia ponds; milkfish pond in diluted seawater, 23 ppt)
scale: One FPV-covered and one control pond at each of 3 Taiwan Fisheries Research Institute sites (Chupei and Lukang ~800 m2, 1 m deep; Cigu ~3000 m2, 1.75 m deep)
dose: Hydrelio HDPE floating PV buoys covering 40% of the pond surface
result: Mean plankton biomass in control ponds was at least twice that in FPV ponds at all three sites (p<0.05; e.g. 12,923 vs 5052 units/L at Chupei, 19,597 vs 7683 at Lukang, 136 vs 43 at Cigu), and BOD was lower under FPV. Final production was 1.1x (prawn), 1.2x (tilapia) and 1.41x (milkfish) higher in FPV ponds.
env_effects: FPV ponds had higher total ammonia nitrogen (significant at Chupei: 0.203 vs 0.037 ppm) and higher orthophosphate (significant at Chupei and Cigu), while total photosynthetic pigments were lower (significant at Lukang and Cigu).
key_details: Paired-pond field comparison at three aquaculture sites: each site had one pond with 40% simulated floating-photovoltaic cover and one uncovered control, both aerated by paddle wheels and stocked identically (20,000 prawns, 5,000 tilapia or 3,700 milkfish). Water quality was sampled repeatedly (n=11, 12 and 6 sampling events), so replication is temporal only with one pond per treatment (pseudoreplication). Plankton biomass fell by about 61%, 61% and 68% (computed from Table 2 means) and total photosynthetic pigments by 35-88%. Survival was 30.9 vs 30.0% (prawn), 48 vs 40% (tilapia) and 66.4 vs 40.7% (milkfish).
fulltext_discrepancy: effect_pct was null; Table 2 gives about a 61% lower plankton biomass under 40% FPV cover (computed from means). The record also omits the higher ammonia and orthophosphate in FPV ponds, and the design has only one pond per treatment per site.

title: Floating solar panels on reservoirs impact phytoplankton populations: A modelling experiment
authors: Exley G, Page T, Thackeray SJ, Folkard AM, Couture R-M, Hernandez RR
scale: MyLake-FPV 1-D model of a UK two-tank reservoir (existing 4.5% FPV array), 0-100% extra coverage in 10% steps, three siting scenarios (fast-flowing tank, central, slow-flowing tank), with uncertainty (GLUE-style) ensembles
result: Peak total chlorophyll-a declined roughly exponentially with coverage: in Scenario-Fast by 10.21 ug/L at 10% cover, 20.40 at 50% and 22.09 at 90% (negligible chl-a above 60% cover); Scenario-Central by 4.01, 19.69 and 22.01 ug/L. With the slow-tank siting, up to 30% cover gave anything from a 19% decrease to a 4% increase.
env_effects: Altered thermal structure; species composition changes.
key_details: Modelling only, no field validation of FPV effects (no published values existed for FPV effects on wind or light, so they were assumed). Phytoplankton simulated as three functional groups (diatoms, cyanobacteria, greens; grazed/ungrazed). FPV mostly cooled surface water (Tmax -0.55 C per 10% cover up to 70% in Scenario-Fast), with a few warmer days at low cover. Total cyanobacteria biomass fell with coverage, but authors warn functional-group aggregation could miss shade-tolerant species becoming dominant.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record gave no magnitudes; full text shows large chlorophyll cuts only at high coverage and possible increases at low coverage in one siting.

title: Impacts of a floating photovoltaic system on temperature and water quality in a shallow tropical reservoir
authors: Yang P, Chua LHC, Irvine KN, Nguyen MT, Low E-W
scale: Tengeh Reservoir, Singapore: field sampling at 6 sites (May 2015-May 2017), 6 m2 mock-up and 1 ha demonstration FPV (2017) for temperature, pH, DO and radiation; 3-D ELCD model predicting a hypothetical 30 MW (42 ha) array
result: Model predicted chlorophyll-a under panels to decline by up to 30%, with water ~0.3 °C warmer and a more stable water column (Richardson number 2.3 to 3.3). Away from the panels, water quality was unaffected.
env_effects: Model: DO under panels down up to 50%, TOC down 15%, TN +10% and TP +30%, mixing energy 9e-7 to 7e-7 W/kg. Measured under the 1 ha demo: DO 7.96 mg/L (105% sat.) vs 8.48 mg/L (111%) in open water, higher pH, surface water +0.32 C on average.
key_details: The 30% chlorophyll-a decline is a model prediction for the hypothetical 42 ha installation, not a measurement; the field demo measured physical/chemical variables only (no chlorophyll comparison reported). Model was calibrated/validated against the 2015-2017 field sampling. Effects were confined to the area under the panels. Tropical reservoir setting.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record said the model was 'validated with a 1 ha demo'; the model was validated against 2015-2017 field sampling, and the demo supplied temperature, radiation, pH and DO only, so the 30% chlorophyll cut is purely modelled.

title: Viability of the cyanobacterium Planktothrix rubescens in the cold and dark, related to over-winter survival and summer recruitment in Lake Zürich
result: After 58 days of cold darkness, filament viability ranged from 0% (strain 9307) to >50% (strains 9736 and 97112). In the hardiest strain viability was 93% at 34 days, 38% at 79 days and 0% at 111 days, with 50% mortality estimated at 70 days.
key_details: Six P. rubescens strains isolated from Lake Zurich (1993-1997) were stored at 4 C in the dark, then single filaments were transferred to 20 C light and scored for regrowth. Population-culture tests (Method A) were abandoned because many filaments lysed and could not be picked. Single-filament tests used 36 filaments per strain at 58 days, and 72 filaments per time point in the time course for strain 9736. Integrated mean survival over 111 days was 61%. The study concerns over-winter survival, not a mitigation treatment, and relevance to shading-based control is indirect.
fulltext_discrepancy: The record's '4-5 C' should be 4 C. Full loss of viability in the hardiest strain took 111 days (~16 weeks) of total darkness.
